script.title: How the scam actually worked: the 'bail money' calls from Montreal
script.hook: 25 people charged, more than 40 states, more than $21 million. This is how prosecutors say one grandparent scam network ran.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: Imagine the phone rings at your grandmother's house. Grandma, it's me. I was in a car accident, and I've been arrested. Please don't tell Mom. A few minutes later a lawyer calls with the amount for bail. A few hours later someone knocks on the door to collect it in cash. According to federal prosecutors, a version of that call was made again and again, for about three years, from call centers in and around Montreal. In March 2025, twenty-five Canadian nationals were charged. Prosecutors say the scheme took more than twenty-one million dollars from older Americans in Vermont and more than forty other states. These are charges, not convictions, so everyone named is presumed innocent. But the method is laid out in the public record, and it's worth knowing in detail.

segments.heading: Step 1: the grandchild
segments.narration: Step one is the call. The caller claims to be a relative, usually a grandchild, who has been arrested after a car crash and needs bail. The details are vague on purpose. Scammers don't need to know your grandchild's name if the grandparent says it first: is that you, Michael? Yes, it's me. The panic does the rest.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the lawyer
segments.narration: Step two, the indictment alleges, is a second person posing as the grandchild's attorney. This matters. A second voice, with a calm professional tone and a specific dollar amount, makes the story feel checked. It's also what moves the conversation from feelings to logistics: how much, and how fast.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: the gag order
segments.narration: Step three is secrecy. According to prosecutors, victims were often told there was a gag order, so they couldn't tell anyone about the arrest. That one line does two jobs. It stops the grandparent calling the parents, who would know in ten seconds that the grandchild is fine. And it explains away anything odd, because the courts said so.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: the courier
segments.narration: Step four is the knock at the door. Victims allegedly handed cash to someone posing as a bail bondsman who came to their home. Notice why that's clever. A bank teller might ask questions about a large wire. Nobody asks questions about an envelope handed over at your own front door.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 5: the money
segments.narration: Step five is moving the money. The indictment alleges the cash was sent to Canada through cash deliveries and financial transactions, sometimes involving cryptocurrency, to hide where it came from and who had it. By the time a family finds out, the money has usually crossed a border.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One afternoon, from the inside
segments.narration: Let's put the steps together in one afternoon. This is a made-up composite, not a person from the court record. Helen is seventy-nine and lives alone in Vermont. At one o'clock her phone rings: 'Grandma, it's me.' She says, 'Danny?' and the caller says yes. He's crying, there was a crash, he's been arrested, and please don't tell his mom.
segments.on_screen_text: A composite, not a real victim
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older woman in a farmhouse kitchen answering a landline, snow outside the window. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The lawyer's numbers
segments.narration: At one fifteen a calm man calls, says he's Danny's lawyer, and gives a case number. Bail is nine thousand dollars. Because the other driver was pregnant, there's a gag order, so she mustn't discuss it with anyone, including the bank. A bondsman will come to the house at four. Helen drives to the bank and tells the teller the cash is for a new roof.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a woman at a bank counter with an envelope, a teller looking concerned. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The knock, and the second call
segments.narration: At four a young man in a polo shirt collects the envelope at the door and thanks her. At six the lawyer calls back: the other driver lost the baby, the charge is now more serious, and bail is another fifteen thousand. That second call is common in these schemes, because a person who has paid once has shown they believe the story.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a front door at dusk with an envelope being handed over, a phone ringing on a table. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where it could have stopped
segments.narration: Now go back through the afternoon and find the exits. At one o'clock: hang up and call Danny's own number. At one fifteen: ask for the family safe word, or call his mom anyway, gag order or not. At four: no court or bail office sends a courier for cash. Any one of those ends it. In this composite, Helen's neighbour sees the second courier and asks what's going on, and that's what finally stops it, nine thousand dollars too late.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a timeline with three exit signs, a neighbour talking with an older woman at a fence. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it came apart
segments.narration: So how did it come apart? On June 4, 2024, Canadian police executed search warrants at several call centers and, according to the release, found many of the defendants in the middle of placing calls to older victims in Virginia. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, IRS Criminal Investigation, and Canadian police, with help from many other agencies. Nine other people had already been charged in Vermont in connection with the same scheme.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Here are the three checks that break every step. One: hang up and call the grandchild, or their parent, on a number you already have. That alone ends almost every version of this call. Two: a family safe word, agreed in person, that anyone calling in a panic has to say. Three: no court, lawyer or bail bondsman sends a stranger to your house to collect cash. If someone is coming to the door, call the police. And if it already happened, report it to the police and to the FBI's IC3, and tell the family. Shame keeps people quiet, and quiet is how the next call works.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: The $26 million pop-up: how fake virus scans sold 'repairs'
script.hook: 1 pop-up, 1 'free scan', and the scan found problems no matter what. The FTC case behind it ended in a $26 million settlement.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: You're reading a news site, and a window pops up that looks like Windows itself. Your computer may be infected. Scan now to avoid more damage. You click, a scan runs, and it finds problems. Lots of them. According to the Federal Trade Commission, scans like this one found problems regardless of the actual condition of the computer. In March 2024, the two companies behind them, Restoro and Reimage, both based in Cyprus, agreed to pay twenty-six million dollars to settle the FTC's charges. Here's how the FTC says it worked, step by step.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: the pop-up
segments.narration: Step one is the pop-up. The FTC says the companies used pop-ups that imitated Windows security warnings and urged people to run a scan to avoid more damage. The trick is borrowing trust. You already believe Windows warnings, so the fake one inherits that belief.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the scan
segments.narration: Step two is the scan. It looks technical, with progress bars and long lists of files, and it always finds something. The FTC alleged the scans flagged serious problems no matter what state the computer was really in. A test that can't come back clean isn't a test. It's a sales pitch with a progress bar.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: cheap software
segments.narration: Step three is a small purchase. The software typically cost between twenty-seven and fifty-eight dollars, according to the FTC. That's low enough that people buy it just to make the warnings stop. But the low price is the hook, not the business.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: the phone call
segments.narration: Step four is the call. After buying, people were told to call a number to activate the software. On the call, telemarketers accessed the computer and, the FTC says, pointed to routine errors, the ordinary messages every computer logs, as signs of viruses or malware. Then the pitch: the software alone can't fix this, you need a technician, and that costs hundreds of dollars more.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why it works
segments.narration: Look at the shape of it. A scary warning, a test that always fails, a cheap first step, then a person on the phone with access to your screen. Each step is small. Nobody decides to pay hundreds for a fake repair. They decide to click a scan, then to spend thirty dollars, then to make one phone call.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One evening, step by step
segments.narration: Here's the whole funnel in one evening. A made-up composite, not a person from the FTC's case. Ray is sixty-eight and reading the news on his laptop when a window that looks like a Windows alert says his computer may be infected. He clicks scan. A progress bar runs and lists hundreds of 'issues', some in red. He buys the fix for about thirty-nine dollars, which feels sensible.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older man at a laptop in a den, a fake system alert window with a progress bar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The activation call
segments.narration: The software asks him to call a number to activate it. A friendly technician asks to connect to his computer to 'make sure it installed'. He opens a system log Ray has never seen, full of warnings and errors, the routine messages every computer collects, and says it's worse than they thought. Hackers may already be in. The full repair and protection plan is a few hundred dollars more.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone call with a technician icon, a screen full of error messages, a worried user. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What Ray's daughter saw
segments.narration: Ray pays. When his daughter visits that weekend, she runs the security tool already built into his computer, and it finds nothing serious. The only new things on the machine are the purchased program and the remote access tool the technician left behind. She uninstalls both, changes his passwords, and calls his card company to dispute the charges.
segments.on_screen_text: A clean computer, a big bill
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a daughter at her father's laptop removing two programs, a phone call to a card company. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where it could have stopped
segments.narration: The exits were early. A pop-up that tells you to scan or call isn't a real security warning, so close the tab. A scan that can't come back clean isn't a test. And never give remote access to someone you reached from a pop-up. In this composite, a card dispute might get some money back. In the real case, the FTC's refunds did that for many people, years later.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a browser tab being closed, a padlock over a remote access icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why Ray didn't feel scammed
segments.narration: Notice that at no point did Ray feel he was being scammed. Running a scan felt careful. Thirty-nine dollars felt modest. Calling to activate software felt normal. Letting a technician look felt helpful. The bad decision was spread across four small, sensible-looking ones. That's why the best defence is a rule made in advance: no pop-up gets my money or my screen.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: four small stepping stones leading to a large hole, an older man stepping carefully. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What happened next
segments.narration: The settlement requires the companies to pay twenty-six million dollars for refunds and bars them from misrepresenting security or performance problems and from deceptive telemarketing. In March 2025, the FTC announced it was sending more than twenty-five and a half million dollars to people affected. On screen is the FTC's refund page for this case.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Three checks stop every version of this. One: real security warnings don't ask you to call a number or buy something from a pop-up. Close the browser tab, and if it won't close, restart the computer. Two: never give remote access to someone you reached through a pop-up or an ad. Three: if you think something's wrong, use the security tools already built into your computer, or take it to a repair shop you chose yourself. Already paid? Call your card company and dispute the charge, and if someone had remote access, change your passwords from a different device.

script.title: How the scam actually worked: the fake invoices that took over $120 million from two tech giants
script.hook: 2 of the biggest tech companies in the world, 1 fake supplier, and over $120 million wired away by email.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: Two of the biggest technology companies in the world. Prosecutors described them only as a multinational technology company and a multinational online social media company. Both were sending millions of dollars to a hardware supplier they'd worked with for years. Between 2013 and 2015, more than one hundred twenty million dollars of those payments went somewhere else. The man behind it, Evaldas Rimasauskas, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and in December 2019 was sentenced to five years in federal prison. Here's how the Justice Department says he did it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: borrow a name
segments.narration: Step one was a name. He registered a company in Latvia with the same name as a real computer hardware maker based in Asia, one the victims really did business with. Then he opened bank accounts in Latvia and Cyprus in that name. So when a payment arrived, the name on the account matched the name on the invoice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the emails
segments.narration: Step two was email. He sent messages to employees and agents at the two companies, made to look like they came from the real supplier's staff, from accounts designed to look genuine. The real supplier never sent them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: the new account
segments.narration: Step three was the ask, and it's always the same ask: please send what you owe to these accounts. Nothing else on the invoice had to change. Same supplier name, same kind of amounts, same kind of request the finance teams handled every week. One line changed: where the money goes. And according to prosecutors, the companies paid.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: move it fast
segments.narration: Step four was speed. Once money landed, he quickly moved it on to accounts in Latvia, Cyprus, Slovakia, Lithuania, Hungary and Hong Kong. When banks asked questions, prosecutors say he gave them forged invoices, contracts and letters that looked signed by executives at the victim companies, with fake corporate stamps.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it ended
segments.narration: Lithuanian authorities arrested him in March 2017, and he was extradited to New York that August. Along with the prison sentence, he was ordered to forfeit about forty-nine point seven million dollars and pay about twenty-six point five million in restitution.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why it matters to you
segments.narration: You might think this only happens to giant companies. It's the opposite. This is the same scam that hits a landlord, a small contractor, or someone buying a house, when an email that looks like the title company says the wiring instructions have changed. The FBI calls it business email compromise, and it reports billions in losses every year. If it worked on two tech giants with whole finance departments, it can work on anyone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The same trick at small scale
segments.narration: Here's the same trick at the size most of us live at. A made-up composite, not part of this case. Priya and Sam are buying their first house. Two days before closing, they get an email that looks like it's from their title company, same logo, same agent's name, saying the wiring instructions for the down payment have changed because of an audit. Please wire sixty-two thousand dollars to the new account today.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a young couple at a laptop with a house key and a closing folder, an email with a logo. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why it looks right
segments.narration: Look at it the way the tech companies' staff saw their invoices. The name matches. The amount matches what they expected. The timing matches. One thing changed: where the money goes. And the sender's email address is one letter off from the real one, which is easy to miss on a phone. Somewhere, someone got into an email thread and waited for the right moment.
segments.on_screen_text: One letter off in the address
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an email address under a magnifying glass with one letter highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The call that saved it
segments.narration: Sam calls the title agent on the number printed on their purchase contract, not the one in the email. The agent says the instructions haven't changed and that they never change instructions by email. Sixty-two thousand dollars stays where it belongs. They forward the email to the title company and report it to the FBI at I C 3 dot gov.
segments.on_screen_text: Call a number you already had
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a man on a phone holding a printed contract, a relieved partner beside him. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If the wire had gone
segments.narration: If the wire had gone out, speed is everything. Call your bank immediately and ask it to recall the wire and contact the receiving bank, then file at I C 3 dot gov the same day. Money that's been moved on, like the payments in this case that went through several countries, gets much harder to recover with every hour.
segments.on_screen_text: Wire sent? Call the bank now
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a clock face with a bank building and an arrow racing toward a border. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rule for your own money
segments.narration: So here's the household version of the companies' fix. Before any big payment, a house deposit, a contractor's final bill, a tuition payment, confirm the account details by voice, on a number you got before the email arrived. Write that number on the folder now, at the start, so you're not hunting for it on the day the pressure is on.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a closing folder with a phone number written on the cover, a pen beside it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Three checks stop it at any size. One: any change to where money goes gets confirmed by a phone call, to a number you already had, never the one in the email. Two: two people sign off on new or changed bank details. Three: slow down on urgency. A real supplier can wait a day for a call back. And if money already went out, call your bank right away and ask them to recall the wire, then report it at the FBI's IC3. Speed matters more than anything else in getting it back.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: 'Google will remove your business': inside the robocalls the FTC stopped
script.hook: 4,467 small business owners got FTC refund checks after robocalls said Google would mark them 'permanently closed'.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: If you've ever run a small business, you've probably had this call. A recorded voice says it's calling about your Google listing. Your business is about to be marked permanently closed. Press one to speak to a Google specialist. In 2018, the Federal Trade Commission went to court to stop one set of companies making these calls, Pointbreak Media and three related companies. Two years later, the FTC mailed refund checks to four thousand four hundred sixty-seven small business owners. Here's how the scheme worked, from the FTC's public record.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: borrow Google
segments.narration: Step one is borrowing a name every business owner cares about. The callers claimed to be acting on Google's behalf. For a restaurant, a plumber or a hair salon, Google is where customers find you. So a call about your Google listing doesn't sound like a sales call. It sounds like an emergency.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the threat
segments.narration: Step two is the threat. Google will label your business permanently closed unless you speak to a specialist. Think about what that means to an owner. Closed means customers drive past. It's the kind of threat that makes you press one before you think.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: the fee
segments.narration: Step three is the fee. Telemarketers said they could claim and verify the business's Google listing and make it show up prominently in search results, for a one-time fee of three hundred to seven hundred dollars. The court found those claims were false. Claiming a basic Google Business Profile is free, and no one can sell you a promised spot at the top of search results.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why it worked
segments.narration: Why did owners pay? Because each piece was close to something true. Listings really can be claimed. Search placement really does matter. Google really does mark some businesses as closed. The scam stitched true pieces into a false story, then added a deadline.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One salon, one call
segments.narration: Let's walk one call through, as a made-up composite, not a business from the FTC's case. Dee runs a two-chair hair salon. On a busy Saturday, a recording says her Google listing will be marked permanently closed. She's between clients and presses one, because closed sounds like the end of her walk-in trade.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a small hair salon with two chairs, a stylist holding a phone between appointments. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The specialist
segments.narration: A friendly 'specialist' says her listing isn't verified and that, for a one-time fee of four hundred ninety-nine dollars, they'll verify it and get her to the top of local search. He can take a card now. Every piece sounds close to true. Listings can be verified. Search position matters. Dee pays, because the cost of losing customers feels bigger.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone call with a headset icon, a card being read out, a search ranking arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What she finds later
segments.narration: A month later, a regular mentions she found the salon fine on Google, same as always. Dee signs in to her Business Profile herself for the first time and finds it was never at risk, and claiming and managing it is free. Nothing was done for the four hundred ninety-nine dollars. She calls her card company to dispute it and reports the call at the FTC's site.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a laptop showing a business profile with a verified check, a phone call to a card company. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The exits
segments.narration: The exits: Google doesn't robocall you about your listing, so pressing one is the first mistake. Signing in to your own profile answers the question in two minutes. And a fee to keep something that's free is the tell. Put those on a sticky note by the salon phone, because these calls still come, under new names.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a sticky note on a salon phone with three short rules. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The office version, in one week
segments.narration: The same week, Dee gets two more of the patterns from the FTC's small business guide. An invoice for a 'business directory' ad she never ordered, due in fifteen days. And a 'domain renewal' notice from a company that isn't her website host, at three times the price. Same shape: a name she half-recognises, a deadline, a fee. Her new rule handles both. She only pays invoices that match something she ordered, and checks renewals in her own host account.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a desk with two official-looking invoices stamped not ordered, a laptop with a hosting dashboard. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If you already paid
segments.narration: If you already paid one of these, call your card company and dispute it, explaining the service was misrepresented. Report it at the FTC's site, which helps build cases like this one. And tell other business owners on your street or in your trade group, because these calls work through local lists.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone call to a card company, a small group of shop owners chatting on a sidewalk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it ended
segments.narration: The FTC's 2018 action halted the calls, and in August 2020 the agency mailed more than seven hundred thousand dollars in refunds, an average of about one hundred fifty-eight dollars per business. One detail from that refund notice is worth remembering: the FTC never requires payment or information to cash a refund check. If someone says otherwise, that's a second scam.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The office version
segments.narration: These calls still happen, under new names. The FTC's guide for small businesses lists the same pattern for fake directory listings, fake invoices for ads you never ordered, and fake domain renewals. Same shape every time: a name you trust, a threat, a fee.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Three checks for any small business. One: Google doesn't robocall you about your listing. Sign in to your own Business Profile and look. On screen, that's the free sign-up page. Two: one person approves payments, and only for invoices that match something you ordered. Three: if you already paid, call your card company and dispute the charge, and report the call to the FTC. Every report helps them find the next Pointbreak.

script.title: How the scam actually worked: inside the IRS impersonation call centers
script.hook: 24 people sentenced, sentences up to 20 years, thousands of victims. This is how the 'you owe the IRS' calls really worked.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: This is the Internal Revenue Service. There's a warrant for your arrest for unpaid taxes. Pay today, or officers will come to your home. Millions of Americans got a call like that. In 2016, the Justice Department charged dozens of people over one network behind them, and by July 2018, twenty-four had been sentenced in Houston, one to twenty years. The guilty pleas describe, step by step, how the calls turned into cash.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: the call centers
segments.narration: Step one was the call centers, in Ahmedabad, India. According to the pleas, operators used data brokers and other sources to find people in the US to call. That's why the calls sometimes knew your name or your address. It wasn't the IRS's records. It was a purchased list.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the threat
segments.narration: Step two was the threat. Callers posed as officials from the IRS or from US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and told people they faced arrest, prison, fines or deportation unless they paid a government debt immediately. Notice who that targets. Immigrants who fear deportation are less likely to call the police, and that was the point.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: the payment
segments.narration: Step three was payment, by stored value cards or wire transfers. Not a check to the US Treasury, not a payment on IRS dot gov. A card number read over the phone, or a wire to a name you don't know. That payment method is the giveaway, every time.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: the runners
segments.narration: Step four is the part most people never hear about. A network of runners inside the US turned that money into cash, fast. The pleas describe runners buying reloadable cards and sending the card numbers to India, where they were registered using stolen identities of real Americans and loaded with victims' money. Runners then bought money orders, deposited them, picked up wires under fake names with false IDs, and took a cut.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One call, one family
segments.narration: Here's how one call could move through the whole machine, as a made-up composite, not a victim named in the case. Mr. Patel, a recent immigrant, gets a call at nine in the morning. The caller knows his name and address, says he's from the IRS, and says there's an error in his tax filings and an arrest warrant. Then a second voice, from 'immigration', says his status could be affected.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a man in a small apartment taking a phone call, a coffee going cold, morning light. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The payment
segments.narration: They tell him to stay on the line, drive to a store, and buy four prepaid cards worth five hundred dollars each. In the car park, he reads the numbers off the back. Within minutes, according to the way the pleas describe it, numbers like these are sent overseas, loaded onto cards registered with stolen identities, and a runner somewhere in the US is already withdrawing cash or buying money orders.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a man in a car reading numbers from cards into a phone, a map with a fast arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The knock that never came
segments.narration: Officers never come, because there was never a warrant. When Mr. Patel tells a coworker, she shows him the IRS page that says the IRS doesn't demand immediate payment by gift card or prepaid card, and doesn't threaten arrest by phone. He reports it to TIGTA, and calls the card company, which may be able to freeze any balance not yet spent. Most of it is gone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: two coworkers looking at an official website on a phone, a report form on a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where the exits were
segments.narration: The exit was the payment method. The IRS doesn't take gift cards or prepaid cards read over the phone, and no agency asks you to stay on the line while you drive to a store. Notice also who the composite is. The fear of deportation is what made him less likely to check, and less likely to report. If you have neighbours or coworkers new to the country, this is the call to warn them about.
segments.on_screen_text: The tell: how they want paid
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a set of prepaid cards with a large red cross over them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Telling someone new
segments.narration: If you know someone who has recently moved to the US, a coworker, a neighbour, a friend's parent, this is the conversation to have. Tell them three things: the IRS writes first, it never wants gift cards, and immigration officials don't call to collect money. A thirty-second warning from someone they trust is worth more than any website, because the scam works on fear and isolation.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: two neighbours talking over a fence, one showing the other a short note on a phone. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it ended
segments.narration: The investigation was led by Homeland Security Investigations, the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general, and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration. Sentences ranged from probation to two hundred forty months. Twenty-two defendants were held liable for nearly nine million dollars in restitution to identified victims. Thirty-two people and five call centers in India were also charged; they're presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why gift cards
segments.narration: On camera, here's a gift card from a store rack. Read the packaging. Many now print a warning: if someone asks you to pay with this card, it's a scam. That warning is there because of cases like this one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Three checks. One: the IRS generally contacts you by mail first, and doesn't threaten arrest or demand immediate payment by phone. Two: no government agency takes gift cards, prepaid cards or wire transfers to a person. Three: check what you owe yourself, in your IRS Online Account. If you've already paid, call the card company or wire service right away, and report it to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration and the FTC.

script.title: Inside a pig butchering compound: phone farms, scripts and 127,000 bitcoin
script.hook: 127,271 bitcoin, worth about $15 billion: the largest forfeiture action the Justice Department says it has ever brought.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: Hi, is this Jenny? Sorry, wrong number. But you seem nice. That message, and the weeks of friendly chat that follow, ends with an investment app and a balance that can't be withdrawn. In October 2025, federal prosecutors in Brooklyn indicted the chairman of a Cambodian conglomerate called Prince Group, alleging his company ran compounds where trafficked workers were forced to send messages like that one. They also moved to seize about one hundred twenty-seven thousand bitcoin, worth about fifteen billion dollars at the time. These are allegations, and the defendant is presumed innocent. Here's what the public record describes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: the workers
segments.narration: Step one, prosecutors allege, is the workforce. Hundreds of people trafficked into compounds in Cambodia, surrounded by high walls and barbed wire, and forced to run scams, often under threat of violence. That changes how to think about the person texting you. Sometimes they're a prisoner too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: phone farms
segments.narration: Step two is scale. Documents described in the release refer to automated call centers using thousands of phones and millions of mobile numbers. That's why the wrong-number texts never stop. It's not one person. It's industrial.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: trust
segments.narration: Step three is time. Scammers build trust over weeks through messaging apps or social media: daily check-ins, photos, life stories. Nothing is asked for. That patience is what the industry nickname, pig butchering, refers to, and it's why victims don't feel scammed until the very end.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: the investment
segments.narration: Step four is the ask. Not a request for money, an opportunity: a crypto platform where the new friend says they've made money. Small deposits show big gains on a website the scammers control. Then bigger deposits. Then a fee, or a tax, to withdraw, and the money is gone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 5: the laundering
segments.narration: Step five is laundering. The release describes 'spraying' and 'funneling' funds through many accounts, exchanges, online gambling and crypto mining, and alleges luxury purchases including a Picasso. A network in Brooklyn allegedly laundered money from more than two hundred fifty victims in the US.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: From the other side of the chat
segments.narration: Now see it from the phone in your hand. A made-up composite, not a victim named in this case. Ken is fifty-four and divorced. A wrong-number text from 'Anna' turns into a friendship. She sends photos of her dinners and her dog. After three weeks she mentions her uncle's crypto trading platform, and that she's made enough to put a deposit on a flat.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a man on a couch smiling at a phone, a chat with a photo of a dinner and a dog. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The numbers on the screen
segments.narration: Ken signs up through her link and deposits five thousand dollars. Within two weeks the site shows nine thousand two hundred. He withdraws two hundred, and it arrives, which settles his doubts. Over two months he moves in sixty thousand, including a loan. The site shows a hundred and ten thousand. None of it exists. The numbers are typed into a website the scammers control.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone app with a rising chart and a large fake balance, a small real deposit icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The wall
segments.narration: When Ken asks to withdraw, the account is frozen for a 'compliance review'. Release requires a fifteen percent tax up front. Anna says she'll lend him part of it. Then comes a second fee. Meanwhile, on the other side of the screen, the person typing as Anna may be one of the trafficked workers this case describes, working from a script.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a locked vault icon on a phone, a fee notice, a tired worker silhouette at a desk far away. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The exits
segments.narration: Count the exits, all before the first deposit: a wrong-number text that kept going, a move to private chat, an investment tip from someone he'd never met, and a platform he only reached through her link. And one big one at the end: never pay a fee to withdraw your own money. Ken reports it at I C 3 dot gov with every wallet address and screenshot, which is how cases like this get built.

segments.heading: What Ken's family did

Then she helps him report it, call the lender about the loan, and block every 'recovery agent' who messages him over the next month, offering to get the money back for a fee. They're the same industry, working the same list of victims, and they're the reason the second loss often follows the first. Real law enforcement doesn't charge a fee to look into your case, and a stranger who knows exactly what you lost is a reason for more caution, not less.

script.title: How the scam actually worked: the money transfer company that paid $586 million
script.hook: $586 million. That's what Western Union agreed to forfeit in 2017 after scammers used its system for years.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: Every part of this series so far has had a scammer at the center. This one doesn't. It's about the pipe the money flowed through. In January 2017, Western Union agreed to a five hundred eighty-six million dollar judgment with the Federal Trade Commission, and to forfeit the same amount under an agreement with the Justice Department. It admitted to willfully failing to keep an effective anti-money laundering program, and to aiding and abetting wire fraud. Here's what the public record says happened.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why money transfers
segments.narration: First, why scammers love money transfers. Lottery scams, grandparent scams, romance scams, fake IRS calls: for years, the instructions were the same. Go to a store, send the money by transfer, read me the reference number. It's fast, it reaches almost any country, and once it's picked up, it's very hard to reverse.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: the agents
segments.narration: Step one in the FTC's account is the agents, the stores and counters that handle transfers. The FTC alleged that fraudsters worldwide used the system for years, that some agents were complicit, and that the company profited by not promptly suspending or terminating the problem ones.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the reports
segments.narration: Step two is the paper trail. Starting in at least 2004, the FTC says, the company logged customer complaints about fraud-induced payments. That same year, its own security department proposed automatically suspending any agent who paid out fifteen fraud reports within one hundred twenty days. The FTC says that rule would have led to action against more than two thousand agents worldwide between 2004 and 2012.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: the fixes
segments.narration: Step three is the order. It requires a comprehensive anti-fraud program, blocking transfers to anyone who's the subject of a fraud report, refunds when the company fails to follow its anti-fraud procedures, and clear fraud warnings on transfer forms. On camera, that's the kind of warning you'll now see on a form. Read it before you send money to anyone you haven't met.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The refunds
segments.narration: Then the part most people missed: victims could get money back. The Justice Department ran a compensation program for people who sent money to scammers through Western Union, and paid it out in rounds, including about one hundred fifty-three million dollars in March 2020 and one hundred forty-seven million in September 2020. Legitimate refund programs like this never charge you a fee to claim.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The lesson
segments.narration: The lesson isn't that one company is bad and the others are safe. It's that the way you pay decides whether you can get money back. A credit card has dispute rights. A transfer picked up in cash usually doesn't.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One transfer, followed
segments.narration: Let's follow one transfer through the pipe. A made-up composite, not a person from this case. Joan, seventy-two, is told on the phone that she's won a large lottery prize in another country, but must first pay taxes and fees. The caller tells her to go to a store and send nine hundred dollars by money transfer to a 'customs officer', and read back the reference number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older woman at a store counter filling out a money transfer form, a phone in her other hand. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: At the counter
segments.narration: At the counter, the form has a fraud warning on it, and the clerk could ask who she's sending to and why. In this version, he doesn't. Joan sends it, reads the number to the caller, and within minutes the money is picked up in cash somewhere else. Two days later, a new call: more fees, another transfer. That pattern, repeated payouts tied to fraud reports, is what the FTC's case was about.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a counter with a transfer receipt, a cash pickup happening in a distant city. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What changes after the order
segments.narration: After the order, the system is meant to work differently. Transfers to people who've been reported for fraud get blocked. Agents with too many fraud reports face action. And the form's warning is there for the moment Joan is standing at the counter. If she'd told the clerk it was for a prize, a well-trained agent should stop and explain that real prizes don't charge fees.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a transfer form with a warning box highlighted, a clerk speaking kindly to a customer. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What Joan should do
segments.narration: And Joan herself? The fastest move is to call the transfer company the moment she realises, because until the money is picked up, it can sometimes be stopped. Then report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. And the rule for next time: anyone who tells you to pay a prize fee, by transfer, gift card or crypto, is the scam.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a woman on the phone with a transfer receipt, a stop sign over a cash pickup icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If you're the family
segments.narration: If you look after an older parent's money, here's a simple habit. Ask kindly about any money transfer, gift card purchase or crypto ATM visit, not to police them, but because those three are how most of these scams get paid. A parent who knows you'll ask is a parent who might stop at the counter and call you first.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an adult child and an older parent talking over tea, a receipt on the table. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Three checks. One: anyone who tells you to pay by money transfer, gift card or crypto, and hurry, is the scam. Two: never send a transfer to someone you haven't met in person. Three: if you already sent one, call the transfer company immediately and ask them to stop it, because until it's picked up, it may still be stoppable. Then report it to the FTC, and watch for official refund programs, which you'll find on ftc.gov, not in a text.

script.title: The 'chairmen' behind a $100 million romance scam ring
script.hook: More than $100 million, dozens of victims, and 2 'chairmen' who have now pleaded guilty. This is how the romance scam ring ran.

segments.heading: Cold open
segments.narration: She's a doctor working overseas. He's an engineer on an oil rig. They message every day, for months, and they can never quite video call. In October 2026, two men from Ghana, described by prosecutors as chairmen of a criminal organization, pleaded guilty in Manhattan to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Prosecutors say the group stole and laundered more than one hundred million dollars from dozens of victims. Here's how they say it ran.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: the profile
segments.narration: Step one is the identity. Members assumed fake identities to pose as romantic partners online. The photos are usually stolen from real people. On screen, I'm running a reverse image search on a photo of myself, so you can see how quickly a picture shows up under other names. Try it on any profile that seems too perfect.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: the trust
segments.narration: Step two is time. According to the release, many victims were vulnerable older men and women. The messages come every day. The relationship feels real, because to the victim, it is. That's why we never call people who fall for this foolish. The whole operation is built to beat good judgment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: the money
segments.narration: Step three is money, and it comes in two forms. The first is familiar: send money to the partner, for a ticket, a medical bill, a customs fee. The second is less known. Prosecutors say victims were also persuaded to help launder money taken from other victims: receive this transfer, then send it on. That can pull an innocent person into a criminal investigation.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: the businesses
segments.narration: Step four shows how these groups diversify. The same organization, prosecutors say, also tricked businesses into wiring money, the business email compromise scam from part three of this series. Then the proceeds were laundered back to West Africa.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One relationship, followed
segments.narration: Here's the path one person might take through an operation like this. A made-up composite, not a victim named in the case. Margaret is seventy and widowed. A man who says he's a surgeon with an aid group abroad comments on a photo she posted. They talk daily for four months. His camera is always broken, the connection always too weak for video.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older woman reading messages on a tablet in a sunlit garden, a distant hospital tent icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The first ask, then the second
segments.narration: Month five, his pay is stuck and he needs two thousand dollars for a flight home to meet her. She sends it. Month six, he asks a different kind of favour: a company will deposit money in her account, and she should forward it to his business partner. That's the second form of money the prosecutors describe. Margaret thinks she's helping. She's now moving money taken from other victims.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a bank transfer arrow coming into an account and going straight out again. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The bank calls
segments.narration: Her bank notices money coming in and immediately going out, and freezes the account. A fraud investigator calls and explains, gently, that the deposit came from another scam victim. Margaret is devastated, and frightened that she's in trouble. The investigator's advice: stop sending anything, stop talking to him, report it to the FBI at I C 3 dot gov, and bring in her family.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older woman on the phone at a kitchen table, a bank statement with a lock icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The exits
segments.narration: The exits were there from month one: a profile that never video calls, a move off the platform, and then any request for money from someone she'd never met in person. And one exit people rarely hear: never receive and pass on money for anyone. When a family member asks gently, early, about a new online friend, these stories end in month two, not month six.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a timeline of six months with exit signs at months one, two and five. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If you're Margaret
segments.narration: If you've received and passed on money for an online partner, it's important to know you can stop now, and the bank and law enforcement are the people to tell. Many people in Margaret's position are victims who were deceived, and saying so early, with your messages saved, is far better than waiting. Don't move another dollar for anyone you haven't met. And if you're the family member hearing this for the first time, the first words matter most: thank you for telling me, we'll sort it out together. That sentence keeps the next conversation open.

segments.heading: How it's ending
segments.narration: The two men were extradited to the US in August 2025. One was held responsible for about twelve and a half million dollars in losses, the other for about twenty-eight and a half million. Each faces up to twenty years, though the judge decides the actual sentence. Another member was previously sentenced to eighty-five months, and one remains at large.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: For families
segments.narration: If you're worried about a parent, start with kindness. Ask about the person they're talking to, and listen. Shame is what makes people hide transfers, and hiding is what keeps the money flowing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam with the case board and source document; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three checks
segments.narration: Three checks. One: never send money, gift cards or crypto to someone you haven't met in person, however long you've talked. Two: never receive and pass on money for someone, which can make you part of a crime. Three: reverse image search their photos, and if they can't do a live video call, assume they're not who they say. If it already happened, report it to the FBI's IC3 and the FTC, and tell your bank about any transfers.
